title: Why You Get Goosebumps
sources: Wikipedia, Goose bumps (piloerection: arrector pili contraction via the sympathetic nervous system; triggered by cold and strong emotions; in furry animals it traps insulating air and makes the animal look larger; largely vestigial in humans) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goose_bumps

Why Evolution Is True, 'Vestigial trait: the arrector pili' (raised fur in cats and other mammals; human goosebumps as a leftover) https://whyevolutionistrue.com/2011/02/22/vestigial-trait-the-arrector-pili

Durham University repository: piloerection may still play a small role in human thermoregulation (not purely vestigial; little empirical research) https://durham-repository.worktribe.com/OutputFile/2743976

lines.text: You hear one perfect song, and your arms explode in tiny bumps.
Here's why. Every hair on your skin has its own tiny muscle.
When you get cold, or a feeling hits you hard,
lines.caps: WHEN YOU GET *COLD | OR A *FEELING | HITS YOU *HARD

lines.text: your nervous system flips into alert mode,
and thousands of those muscles squeeze at once, pulling every hair straight up.
The skin around each one bunches into a bump.
For a furry animal, that's a superpower.
Puffed-up fur traps warm air, and makes it look bigger to a threat.
A scared cat does exactly this.
But you lost most of your fur, so you're mostly left with the bumps,
lines.caps: YOU LOST | YOUR *FUR | LEFT WITH THE *BUMPS

lines.text: a leftover from your furry ancestors,
still firing every time a song gives you chills.
lines.caps: STILL *FIRING | EVERY TIME | A SONG GIVES *CHILLS
